title: No difference
hookLine: Nagarjuna's well-known line: no difference between samsara and nirvana (Mulamadhyamakakarika 25)
last: A SNAKE PICKED UP BY THE WRONG END.

cards: Two words have run underneath this whole path. Samsara: the wheel of birth and death, craving and suffering, round and round. Nirvana: the fire gone out, the wheel stopped, peace.

Much of this path has followed the teaching from the first toward the second. Then, near the end of his Root Verses, Nagarjuna writes a line that seems to erase the distance. There's no difference between them, he says.

teach.b: It's in chapter twenty-five, on nirvana. Samsara has not the slightest difference from nirvana, Nagarjuna writes, and nirvana has not the slightest difference from samsara.
Then he presses further: the limit of nirvana is the limit of samsara, and between the two there's not even the finest gap. How can he say it? Through yesterday's two truths.
In ultimate terms, samsara and nirvana are both empty. Neither is a thing standing on its own, a place you leave or a place you arrive. Nirvana isn't a far country with a border to cross.

Now, what the line doesn't say. It doesn't say nothing needs to change, or that craving is already peace. The chapter itself closes by calling peace the stilling of all grasping and all spinning thoughts.
The difference he denies is between two separate, solid realms.
The work of seeing clearly remains. Readers hear it in different ways.

teach.h: READ THROUGH LOGIC, READ AT HOME.
teach.b: Madhyamaka teachers in India and Tibet read the line through emptiness, with careful logic.

In East Asia, some Zen and other Mahayana teachers heard in it something close to home: awakening is found here, in the kitchen and the market, not somewhere else. Each reading takes the line seriously in its own way.
And it leaves one question for an ordinary afternoon. If the sacred isn't somewhere else, where is it right now?

how: Mahayana Buddhists study Nagarjuna's chapter on nirvana in monastic colleges and teaching programs, and some Zen and other East Asian teachers speak of finding awakening in ordinary daily activity.

games.q: you've just read that samsara and nirvana have not the slightest difference. a friend says, "so I can stop practicing." what does the chapter suggest?
o: yes, there's nothing left to do.
no: the line denies two solid realms, not the work of seeing clearly.
no: the line must be a copying mistake.
games.why: the difference Nagarjuna denies is between two separate, solid places. letting go and seeing clearly remain.

practice: Let your eyes or ears rest on the plainest thing near you, a spoon, a doorframe, the sound of traffic, your own breath.
Don't make it special or holy by thinking hard; just give it the kind of attention you might give in a temple or under a great tree. Let it be ordinary, and let it be enough.

wordCard.voice: No difference. Nagarjuna's line that samsara and nirvana have not the slightest difference, since both are empty of standing on their own. Today's word.

orig.note: Sanskrit samsara: the wandering on, the round of birth and death.

carryVoice: Your line: not even the finest gap. Samsara and nirvana, side by side, with nothing between. See you tomorrow.
